claims.text: High-temperature stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is not governed solely by configurational entropy.
Local chemical bonding and diffusion barriers predominantly govern high-temperature stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Increasing local bond strength and diffusion barriers inhibits atomic rearrangements that cause phase decomposition and chemical segregation.
The proposed initial nanoalloy is nearly homogeneous, metastable, and single phase after rapid synthesis.
A constituent can be replaced by an element of similar atomic size but stronger bonding and higher diffusion barriers while leaving configurational entropy nearly unchanged.
Elemental substitution can alter phase-decomposition behavior during annealing.
Atomic diffusion becomes pronounced in the proposed high-temperature test regime.
The substituted element raises local bond strength and diffusion barriers.
Higher local bond strength and diffusion barriers reduce the rate of atomic diffusion.
Suppressing atomic mobility inhibits phase decomposition and grain-boundary formation.
Suppressing atomic mobility minimizes selective elemental segregation at high temperature.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will show a later onset of phase decomposition.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit less grain coarsening.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will exhibit less chemical segregation.
The baseline has lower local bond strength and lower diffusion barriers and therefore develops phase instability and segregation earlier.
The predicted benefit is limited to regimes in which diffusional processes govern instability.
At low temperatures, minimal diffusion makes enhanced bond strength unlikely to substantially alter stability.
Enthalpic or solution-thermodynamic contributions may also influence phase stability.
A specific elemental substitution can affect phase stability and other alloy properties.
